justification: The article delivers on its stated angle and does so honestly: the closing measurement table (500 to 200,000 words) shows the sorted array beating the trie on both memory and per-query time at every tested size with the gap widening, not narrowing, as n grows — and the prose is careful to scope the claim to the tested range ('Looking for a crossover assumes one exists in this range. It does not') rather than asserting a universal law, which avoids exactly the unscoped-absolute pitfall the brief's pilot-round lessons flag. This is a genuine, checkable differentiator: fetched this round, neither Wikipedia's Trie page nor GeeksforGeeks's trie-insert-and-search page contains any measured comparison against a sorted array at all — both make only qualitative memory-cost admissions with no numbers, confirming that the honest, benchmarked framing here is not something a reader gets from the current top results for this topic. The article does not oversell the trie's loss either: the penultimate section explicitly names when a trie (specifically the compressed/radix form) is still the right call — cursor-persisting keystroke-by-keystroke queries, wildcard/edit-distance search, small alphabets with heavy sharing — so the piece reads as a genuine trade-off analysis rather than either 'tries are magic' or 'tries are useless.' No filler: the opening paragraph gives a concrete multi-example scenario (contacts list, code editor, shell tab-completion) and states the article's actual plan in its last sentence, with no restated title, no 'in this article,' and no boilerplate Introduction/Conclusion/Key-takeaways heading; the closing section ('Picking one for a real autocomplete box') ends on a concrete decision rule, not a summary that repeats the headings. Headings are specific to the content and do not template-match sibling data-structures articles (checked against binary-search-trees.md and heaps-and-priority-queues.md headings — no overlap, no reused phrasing). issues.location: "What a trie costs in memory" section (the id=trie-memory-small block and the paragraph starting "One run on this machine: 50 synthetic words used 0.5 KB..."), and the "Does sharing more of the prefix change the outcome?" exercise's solution (the id=trie-extreme-sharing block and "On one run: 11.8 KB for the array, 81.3 KB for the trie...")
issues.problem: These are the article's first and second measured sections — both print real GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread byte counts from an actual run — but neither states or is near a statement of the toolchain that produced them. The only toolchain statement in the whole article ('.NET 10.0.12 on Windows 11, build 22631, 16 logical processors') appears much later, near the third measured section (the 500-to-200,000-word benchmark table). EDITORIAL_BRIEF.md's binding pilot-round lessons require the toolchain to be stated 'where measurements appear,' specifically so a reader can judge whether a reported number is a property of the algorithm/runtime or an artifact of one unspecified machine — and that concern applies fully to allocated-byte counts, which are themselves runtime-version-dependent (object header size, Dictionary<TKey,TValue>'s internal bucket/entry array layout can change across .NET versions). A reader who stops at the first hard numbers in the piece (0.5 KB vs. 69.8 KB, ~146x) has no way to know what produced them until roughly 250 lines later. This is the same class of finding that capped the sibling p-vs-np article's score, though less severe here because the statement does exist once in the article, just not adjacent to its first appearance.
